title: Joseph's Farewell
overview: Genesis 50 concludes the Joseph narrative with the death of Jacob and Joseph’s faithful fulfillment of his father’s burial wishes. This chapter highlights themes of forgiveness, divine providence, and covenant faithfulness. Joseph’s leadership and grace are evident as he comforts his fearful brothers and reassures them of God’s sovereign plan. The chapter also sets the stage for Israel’s future in Egypt, emphasizing God’s ongoing promises to the patriarchs. Through mourning, burial, and reconciliation, Genesis 50 powerfully illustrates God’s redemptive work amid human frailty and the continuation of His covenant promises.
structure:
**Verses 1-14: The Death and Burial of Jacob.** This section details Joseph’s mourning, embalming, and the elaborate burial of Jacob in Canaan, fulfilling his father’s last request. The narrative emphasizes respect for family and covenantal land.

**Verses 15-21: Joseph’s Brothers Fear Retribution and Are Forgiven.** After Jacob’s death, Joseph’s brothers fear vengeance for their past sins, but Joseph reassures them, highlighting God’s providential use of their evil intentions for good.

**Verses 22-26: Joseph’s Later Life and Death.** The chapter closes with Joseph’s life in Egypt, his death at 110 years, and his instructions for his bones to be carried to the promised land, affirming hope in God’s future deliverance.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God?
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals Joseph’s humility and recognition that judgment belongs to God alone, underscoring the theme of forgiveness and divine sovereignty in human affairs.

keyVerses.text: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
keyVerses.significance: This key verse encapsulates the doctrine of providence, showing how God can use human sin and evil intentions to accomplish His redemptive purposes.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.
keyVerses.significance: Joseph’s prophetic assurance of God’s future deliverance affirms the faithfulness of God’s covenant promises to the patriarchs and the hope of Israel’s eventual redemption.

characters.name: Joseph
characters.description: The favored son of Jacob who rises to power in Egypt. In this chapter, he faithfully fulfills his father’s burial wishes, forgives his brothers, and reassures them of God’s providence and protection.

characters.name: Jacob (Israel)
characters.description: The patriarch whose death and burial conclude the Genesis narrative. His instructions for burial in Canaan affirm the importance of the promised land in God’s covenant.

characters.name: Joseph’s Brothers
characters.description: They fear retribution after Jacob’s death due to their past betrayal of Joseph. Their repentance and Joseph’s forgiveness highlight themes of reconciliation and grace.

themes.description: Joseph’s statement that God turned evil intentions into good (v. 20) illustrates God’s sovereign control over history, a key biblical theme showing that God works through human actions to fulfill His purposes.
Joseph’s forgiveness of his brothers despite their past sins demonstrates the power of grace and restoration, reflecting the broader biblical call to forgive as God forgives.
The burial of Jacob in Canaan and Joseph’s oath to carry his bones back reflect the ongoing trust in God’s promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob concerning the land and future deliverance.

historicalContext: Genesis 50 is set in the late Bronze Age, likely around the 18th century BC, during the time of the patriarchs. The narrative takes place primarily in Egypt and Canaan, two key geographical regions. Egyptian customs such as embalming and elaborate mourning rituals are evident, reflecting the cultural context of Joseph’s high status in Pharaoh’s court. Politically, Egypt was a dominant power, and Joseph’s role as a governor illustrates the integration of a Hebrew family into Egyptian society while maintaining their distinct identity and covenantal heritage. The burial in Canaan underscores the importance of land possession and ancestral heritage in ancient Near Eastern culture.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign providence as seen in Joseph’s life and this chapter, highlighting that God ordains even human evil for His glory and the good of His people.
Dispensationalists focus on the literal fulfillment of God’s promises to Israel, noting Joseph’s burial instructions as a foreshadowing of Israel’s eventual exodus and return to the promised land.
Early Church Fathers often saw Joseph as a type of Christ, with this chapter’s themes of forgiveness and salvation prefiguring Christ’s redemptive work and God’s providential care for His people.

crossReferences.connection: Paul’s teaching that God works all things for good echoes Joseph’s declaration in Genesis 50:20 about God’s providential use of evil for good.
The call to commit one’s way to the Lord and trust Him parallels Joseph’s trust in God’s plan despite his brothers’ betrayal.
The exhortation to forgive others as the Lord forgave you reflects Joseph’s forgiveness of his brothers in this chapter.
Joseph’s faith in God’s promises and his instructions regarding his bones are commended as an example of faith in the future resurrection and deliverance.
Moses later carries Joseph’s bones out of Egypt, fulfilling the oath Joseph made in Genesis 50:25.

application: Trust God’s providence even when circumstances seem difficult or unfair, knowing He can bring good from evil.
Practice forgiveness toward those who have wronged you, following Joseph’s example of grace and reconciliation.
Honor family and God’s covenant promises by living faithfully and remembering God’s faithfulness.
Comfort others with words of hope and assurance rooted in God’s sovereignty and care.
Live with a forward-looking faith, like Joseph, confident in God’s future deliverance and promises.
Commit to obeying God’s instructions fully, as Joseph did in burying his father according to his wishes.
conclusion: Genesis 50 powerfully concludes the Joseph story by demonstrating God’s providential hand in history, the power of forgiveness, and the faithfulness to covenant promises. Joseph’s compassionate leadership and trust in God’s plan provide a model for believers facing trials and relational challenges. The chapter’s themes encourage Christians to trust God’s sovereignty, extend grace to others, and live in hopeful obedience to His promises, confident that God works all things for the good of His people.

outline.heading: Joseph Mourns and Embalms Jacob
outline.description: Joseph expresses deep grief over his father’s death and commands the Egyptian physicians to embalm Jacob, showing respect and honoring Egyptian customs.

outline.heading: Request and Permission to Bury Jacob
outline.description: Joseph petitions Pharaoh to allow him to bury his father in Canaan as per Jacob’s instructions, and Pharaoh grants permission, highlighting Joseph’s influence.

outline.heading: The Funeral Procession to Canaan
outline.description: A large company, including Egyptian officials and Joseph’s family, accompanies the burial. They mourn deeply, and Jacob is laid to rest in the family tomb, fulfilling the covenantal promise.

outline.heading: Brothers’ Fear and Joseph’s Forgiveness
outline.description: Joseph’s brothers fear retaliation after their father’s death, but Joseph reassures them with forgiveness and explains God’s providential plan to save many lives.

outline.heading: Joseph’s Later Life and Death
outline.description: Joseph lives to an old age, sees his descendants, and dies. He makes the Israelites swear to carry his bones to the promised land, affirming faith in God’s future deliverance.
